claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is equiatomic, single-phase, and FCC in its solidified initial state.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi reduces the stacking-fault energy.
High strain rate or low temperature activates nanotwinning as a competing mechanism to ordinary dislocation glide in Co-free FeNiCrMn.
Nanotwinning enhances work-hardening and delays failure relative to Co-containing CoCrFeMnNi.
Temperature and strain rate govern the competition between deformation twinning and dislocation-network formation.
Altered electronic bonding caused by Co removal shifts stacking-fault energy into a nanotwin-favoring regime.
Lower stacking-fault energy can enable nanotwinning.
Twin boundaries impede dislocation motion and thereby increase work-hardening.
The increased work-hardening associated with nanotwinning raises ductility while maintaining strength.
At higher temperatures or lower strain rates, dislocation glide accompanied by dynamic recovery predominates.
At high strain rate or low temperature, Co-free FeNiCrMn will have a higher twin density than equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi processed and tested comparably.
At high strain rate or low temperature, Co-free FeNiCrMn will exhibit greater work-hardening than the CoCrFeMnNi baseline.
The greater work-hardening of Co-free FeNiCrMn will produce higher ductility with maintained strength relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
Differences between the Co-free and Co-containing alloys will be less pronounced at lower strain rates or higher temperatures.
The prediction is restricted to an FCC, single-phase solid-solution regime without deformation-induced phase transformations or other microstructural instabilities.
A controlled comparison should use identically processed CoCrFeMnNi and FeNiCrMn specimens tested at approximately 77 K and 300 K and at low and high strain rates.
Twin density, dislocation structures, work-hardening rate, strength, ductility, and stacking-fault energy are proposed as measurable discriminants.
The hypothesis is refuted if Co-free FeNiCrMn shows no statistically significant increase in nanotwinning and work-hardening under high-rate or low-temperature conditions relative to CoCrFeMnNi.
The hypothesis is also refuted if inferred stacking-fault energy does not correlate with observed twin formation.
